about: The editor's paper review of RC1, mapped by the conductor: each note with the printed page, the chapter file, the text it points at, who owns the change, and the conductor's reading. His words are in briefs/2026-10-31__rc1-paper-review/.

themes.name: Punchlines first, logistics last
themes.rule: Open every part with content: what was achieved, the idea, a visual. How it was run (dates, decisions, versions, what was added after the day) moves to the end of the chapter or the back of the book, for the reader who wants it.

themes.name: The record is a side effect of how the team works
themes.rule: Never 'we captured the record': the record exists because the team was built for determinism, provenance and memory; the scaffolding and the non-functional requirements are the story. See his forthcoming article 'The Augmented Book'.

themes.name: The talk was not finished
themes.rule: Say the talk needed more rounds and moved too fast from high level to detail; the brakes analogy is a starting point to expand, not a finished argument.

themes.name: Big, visual, and experimented in the book itself
themes.rule: The PDF lab is what he had in mind: a visual representation of the page, on a big stage. Make the visuals big; run experiments in the chapters themselves, a couple per chapter in different sections, until the content is done. An animation in the book gets enough frames to explain it, or a different infographic. Use what print has (colour, images); take the best of the talk's slides, not every slide.

themes.name: Ask of every page: what are we trying to say?
themes.rule: Every page has an objective: an idea to communicate, a paradigm shift for the reader. Counts and logistics that do not serve it go (the giant '9' on page 9).

themes.name: The book teaches the reader to replicate the workflow
themes.rule: The reader ends the book where the editor started it. Every chapter has prompts, examples, case studies and 'do this now' steps (a dedicated Claude team account, GitHub, the first agent is the conductor, a policy, a prompt, a schedule), with small diagrams ('you are here') and QR codes to detailed pages on the site (the augmented book). Start with one agent, not thirty; give it bit by bit. A section on building your own presentation UI: the tool is built as the work is made, and reused. The Gen ZX book's content may be reused. Say it personally: 'my objective is to get you to where I am'.

themes.name: Footnotes, links and QR codes: the book is augmented
themes.rule: Times and who-did-what go to footnotes. Sprinkle the book with references to the editor's articles (newsroom.sgit.ai and the other sgit.ai sites), as a short name at the foot of the page or a small QR code (experiment for the smallest size a phone reads). A catalogue of the best articles, content and vaults, and a graph of their cross-references.

themes.name: Wardley maps: shown before they are explained
themes.rule: Mention Wardley maps and introduce them without explaining them; start with smaller, simpler maps (even a graph, then positioned), with side notes on the page for terms as they appear (genesis, custom-built, town planners), with a couple of examples. Explorers, villagers and town planners come later; the advanced idea (the talk an explorer, the book a villager, the publisher a town planner) comes much later, and with a diagram more than words.

themes.name: Provenance lives online; the book is content
themes.rule: The 'Where this came from' sections are at once too detailed (a wall of paths and commits the reader cannot use) and too light (they link nowhere). Provenance of every idea, page and paragraph is kept, as a graph, in the augmented online version (an iPad-like PDF view with augmented capability), not printed in the book.

themes.name: Maps the editor's way: anchored, evidenced, fractal, of anything
themes.rule: A map is a top-down tree or graph that becomes a map when position has meaning (a threat model is a graph because position does not matter). Start from an anchor, a point of view; 'a user and a need' is Simon Wardley's recommendation because people forget the user, not a rule. Every dot links to its facts, evidence, assumptions, or the next map: a dot in one map becomes a map in the next (fractal), a power to show with visuals and animation. Maps of anything you can make a tree of (systems, risk, vulnerabilities, types); evolution axes vary (his newsroom article shows seven or eight kinds), not only genesis, custom-built, product, commodity. Never say 'a map, not a measurement'. Tell the story with maps first; the punchline at the end of the section: 'you are already reading Wardley maps'. Explorers, villagers, town planners told as the story of a passage found, a village built, a town that scales (1, 50, 1,000, 200,000).

themes.name: Synthetic readers, brutal: why do I need to know this, here?
themes.rule: Every passage is tested by a reader who asks: why do I need this, do I have the context, why is it here, does it make sense to me now. Logistics like 'the maps still to come' fail it.

themes.name: The real reason the team stopped, and the value of constraints
themes.rule: The 95% usage is a footnote: he could have moved to a session with more credits. The team stopped because he was about to go on stage and there was no tested way to take in changes made during the talk: no UX to see the delta (what was new), no workflow guaranteeing nothing would break; hence 'lock V1'. His idea was ahead of the stack, a genesis capability used as if it were a product. The interesting point of the limit is the constraint: having to move between Claude sessions forced better engineering (the handover: a new session closes the old, seals it, replaces the public key, so nobody else can be that agent). Constraints matter; working without them lets bad ways go unnoticed. Open source helps.
themes.source_note: The editor's own account, given 31 October 2026, after the day; not in the record to 298be4e. Quote it as his, dated (the book's rule on material added after the day; O4 said 'the record only', so this needs a line in the revision and perhaps a decision).

themes.name: Show the agents talking: quotes from the record
themes.rule: Explain how the team communicates through the repository (commits and their notes, the mail and the board as files, Issues-FS and the like), and show it: real messages from one agent to another, observations, interesting moments, quoted from the history. The historian digs them out and maps them.

themes.name: The site is the scaffolding
themes.rule: The story is the site: the scaffolding, the workflow, the memory. The agents are productive because they have focus and can read their context, and that comes from the site the team built. Show it with rich, companion-style infographics.
